MIN.title: The Deep-Delver
MIN.tagline: The mountain tires before they do.
MIN.identity: Endurance turned into ore. A miner learns the rock by staying with it, working the face long after the light and the legs of others have given out. There is no sight that finds the vein for you. There is only the swing, and the patience to keep swinging.
MIN.mastery: A Grandmaster works the stone tirelessly, and the rock gives up more to their pick than to any other hand. Where a lesser digger walks out empty, they come back up loaded.
MIN.tip: A skilled cut brings the roof down less often, but no skill makes deep rock safe. The save is a lowered chance, never a promise: rock cut loose from all support still falls on anyone, and a slide already in motion answers to no one. Read the face, keep supports near, and pull the last prop of an overhang only when you are ready to run.

WOO.title: The Forester
WOO.tagline: Leaves the forest richer than they found it.
WOO.identity: The whole circle of the woods: the felling, the planting, and the slow burn that turns wood to fuel. A forester learns to read a stand, to take without emptying it, and to leave saplings that will stand when they are gone.
WOO.mastery: A Grandmaster fells all day without tiring, and lays every trunk within a few degrees of where they aimed it. Above all they are the master collier: charcoal bearing their mark burns hotter and longer, and smiths ask for it by name.
WOO.tip: A tree falls toward the face you cut, not away. Stand to the side and strike the face pointing where you want it down, never the one facing you. A green hand's aim wanders and the trunk can land on them; a master lays it exactly where they mean to, clear of their own feet. The wood is heavy and it does not forgive standing in its path.

FAR.title: The Cultivator
FAR.tagline: Mastery bred into the seed itself.
FAR.identity: The patient science of the seed. A cultivator learns the soil and the season, coaxing a little more from a plot each year, and saving back the best of the harvest to sow again.
FAR.mastery: A Grandmaster's heirloom seed out-yields in any hands for a few generations before the line fades and the village comes back for fresh stock. Their harvest keeps through the winter, and a dying cutting in their hands will often take hold anyway.

FIS.title: The Steward of the Pond
FIS.identity: Not the biggest catch, but the longest-lived water. A steward fishes a pond with a light hand, seeds roe to bring a tired pool back to life, and leaves it able to feed them again next season.
FIS.mastery: A novice fishes a pond dead in an afternoon. A Grandmaster's waters stay stocked for years, and a place to fish them is worth trading for. They take what a water can spare, and never more.
FIS.tip: A pond remembers every fish you take, whether it left on a hook, a spear, or in a basket overnight. Fish a spot hard and it goes quiet; left alone it recovers a little each day, never all at once. Roe cast on tired waters brings fish back sooner, and a steward's roe goes further. A green hand loses bites, lands the small ones, and empties a water without noticing.

COO.title: The Signature Dish
COO.tagline: A meal worth traveling for, and it keeps.
COO.identity: The cook who feeds a journey. Anyone can fill a belly for a day. This trade is the meal that travels well and keeps, the ration still good when you finally need it.
COO.mastery: A Grandmaster's preserves outlast anyone else's, so parties and traders commission them before every long haul. Their name on a crock means the food inside will not have turned.

MET.title: The Maker's Mark
MET.tagline: Their name on the steel outlives the hand that struck it.
MET.identity: The trade the whole Almanac grew from. A smith learns the fire by working it: heating, striking, folding, and cooling, until the metal answers the hammer instead of fighting it. The work is slow and hot, and there is no hurrying it.
MET.mastery: A Grandmaster's mark is struck into every tool they finish, forged or cast, and rides it until the tool is spent. Their fuel goes further at the forge, and their quenched steel holds where a lesser hand's would crack clean through.
MET.tip: A tool comes apart at the bench, and its head remembers both its wear and its maker. Take a tiring tool apart before the binding frays: reforge the head alone to freshen it, then fit it anew. Leave it too long and a worn binding is lost when the tool breaks. The mark and its quality ride the head, so a head kept whole keeps the master's work.

POT.title: The Potter's Mark
POT.tagline: Nothing spoils in a masterwork crock.
POT.identity: The quiet keeper of the larder. A potter learns clay and fire to make the vessels everything else is stored in, and the difference between a good crock and a poor one is measured in seasons.
POT.mastery: Food sealed in a Grandmaster's vessels outlasts food sealed in anyone else's. A masterwork crock is bought once and kept for a lifetime, an heirloom with a thumbprint pressed into the glaze.

GLA.title: The Glassmaker's Mark
GLA.tagline: A Master's glass does not crack.
GLA.identity: Command of a narrow window. Glass forgives nothing: too hot or too cold, and the work is lost. This is the trade of the annealer's patience, the rarest calling on the server, and no one is born to it.
GLA.mastery: Where a novice's melt shatters at the edge of tolerance, a Grandmaster works glass that simply holds. A piece blown in a mold or cast from the crucible carries the maker's name from the moment it is formed.

PAN.title: The Surveyor
PAN.tagline: The map itself is the deliverable.
PAN.identity: Hired knowledge of the ground. A surveyor walks a claim and reads what lies beneath it: which ores, and how deep each one runs. The map they leave behind is the work.
PAN.mastery: A Grandmaster's readings are exact, and they share to the whole group at full fidelity. A village brings them in to walk their claim precisely because no one else could draw the map they leave.
PAN.tip: Work the ground in order. A density scan censuses every block for thirty paces around you: that is your chunk survey, and it reads true for every hand. Found something? Bore before you dig: the drill passes through what is really there, and only a Master reads how deep each ore waits from what it brings up. Underground, node search and the proximity ping guide the pick. And practice at the pan: green hands wash a lot of empty gravel, while a Master feels the river strengthen near a lode.

HUN.title: The Master Hunter
HUN.tagline: Reads the animal before it knows they are there.
HUN.identity: The reader of living country. A hunter learns to see an animal at range for what it is, to move unseen, and to take it cleanly enough that nothing of it is wasted.
HUN.mastery: A novice sees a deer, spooks it, and loses it. A Grandmaster reads its size, its condition, and its heading from forty paces, walks a quarter closer than anyone else before it startles, and follows a wounded animal down a trail that lasts half again as long.
HUN.tip: Green hands spook the game from twice as far and waste half the carcass to clumsy knife work; practiced hands walk closer, dress cleaner, and their snares hold what they catch. Work the whole trade and not only the kill: dressing, trapping, butchery and the tanning that follows all fill the same page.

ANI.title: The Master's Line
ANI.tagline: Every calm animal in the valley traces back to their pens.
ANI.identity: The keeper of bloodlines. This trade is not one animal but a line of them, raised and bred across generations toward calm, healthy, dependable stock.
ANI.mastery: A Grandmaster's animals carry their name for life: raised, bred, of the master's line. Closed pens elsewhere breed themselves into sickness, so owners return for fresh outcross blood from the one breeder who keeps a line healthy.

FOR.title: The Master Forager
FOR.tagline: Walks a harvest circuit nobody else can see.
FOR.identity: Private knowledge of the living land. A forager's map is a constellation of small, timed circles: which patches renew, and exactly when each is ready. The knowledge itself is the trade good.
FOR.mastery: A Grandmaster walks a harvest circuit no one else can see or find twice, and they corner the foraged market by selling access to it. What they know is worth more than what they carry.
FOR.tip: Range wide: the first time you take a new species teaches you far more than stripping the same bush ever will. And pick with care, or don't let others pick at all: ground harvested by practiced hands comes back sooner, ground torn up by a novice comes back late. Mind your feet, too. A harvest circuit walked the same way every day wears a trail straight to your best patches, and a trail can be followed. A wise forager varies the route.

ALC.title: The Alchemist's Brand
ALC.tagline: Whose poultice you carry decides whether you get back up.
ALC.identity: Remedies made and branded at the seal. An alchemist learns which things mend and which harm, and puts their name and their intent on every batch that leaves their hands.
ALC.mastery: A Grandmaster's poultice pulls a downed friend further back from the edge than anyone else's, which is why raiders and travelers carry a named brand into danger. Each batch bears its maker and their chosen emphasis: potent, or lasting.

BRE.title: The Brewer's Mark
BRE.identity: The humblest mark, worn in the cellar. Liquids mix and lose their signature, so a brewer's name lives instead on the solid things the cellar keeps: the cured wheel, the aged ham, the barrel that came out right.
BRE.mastery: A Grandmaster's preserves and cures carry their mark, and one sealed barrel in four comes out over the measure it was rated for. The cellar knows its keeper.

TAI.title: The Master Tailor
TAI.tagline: A coat that holds its warmth for years, and their name in the collar.
TAI.identity: Metalworking's twin in cloth. A tailor learns wool and hide and the cut that turns them into warmth, and their name goes into the collar of every garment they finish.
TAI.mastery: A Grandmaster's coats hold their warmth for years where others fray, cut to the maker's choice: warm for the north, cool for the desert, or lasting so the warmth never wears out. Cold-country folk return to the one hand that can keep a coat what it was.

MAS.title: The Mason's Mark
MAS.identity: The oldest mark of all: a stonecutter's personal sigil, struck into the block they dressed and the stone they carved. A mason learns to draw more finished stone from rough rock than it looks able to give.
MAS.mastery: A Grandmaster gets more dressed block from every slab, and their signed carvings carry the mark for the life of the stone. Long after the wall is built, the mark outlasts it.

ENG.title: The Millwright's Mark
ENG.tagline: Machines run truer under their hand, and stay true longer.
ENG.identity: The standing service contract. Machines are built things, and they remember who kept them. A millwright learns the gears and the mechanisms and the slow art of keeping them true.
ENG.mastery: A part a Grandmaster has serviced decays visibly slower until the next hand touches it, so mill owners want no other hand on their machines. Serviced by them, on the mechanism, is the cleanest provenance in the world.

MEL.title: The Master-at-Arms
MEL.tagline: Reads the fight before the first blow lands.
MEL.identity: Not a harder hitter, but a veteran. This trade is read and defense: sizing up a foe before the first blow, planting a shield like a wall, and wearing heavy plate like a second skin.
MEL.mastery: A Grandmaster sees at a glance what a foe is and how close to death, learns by fighting it where a creature is soft and where a blow is wasted, and plants themselves where a lesser fighter breaks. The edge is knowledge and footing, never raw force.

RAN.title: The Marksman's Eye
RAN.tagline: Knows the distance, holds the drop, and the arrow comes back.
RAN.identity: Ballistics by instinct. A marksman learns range and holdover the way a veteran archer judges by eye, and looses with the steadiest hand on the field.
RAN.mastery: A Grandmaster knows the distance, holds the drop without thinking, and makes the shot a novice only hopes for. And the arrow comes back: they recover what a lesser hand leaves in the grass.

TEM.title: The Storm-Warden
TEM.tagline: Keeps the warning everyone else lost.
TEM.identity: The one who stands when the world dissolves. This is the trade of the temporal storm: feeling it coming, weathering it upright, and keeping the wards and translocators of a region running.
TEM.mastery: A Grandmaster keeps the full quarter hour of warning the sky used to give everyone for free, stays standing while novices black out, and runs the region's machinery on the fewest gears. Forecast, resilience, and economy, the rarest kind of calm.

ARC.title: The Archmage
ARC.tagline: Even at the height of the art, the storm can reach back.
ARC.identity: The one trade no one is born to. No calling claims it as its own, though an archivist's habits start them a step ahead. An arcanist learns the art of spells as a discipline, tier by careful tier.
ARC.mastery: A Grandmaster commands the deep workings others cannot reach, but the greatest are never routine: even the Archmage carries a sliver of misfire on the highest spells, and each costs minutes of vulnerable trance to recover. Their trade is the scroll, magic scribed and sold by the charge.

BEE.title: The Hive Warden
BEE.tagline: Sites a hive where it will keep itself.
BEE.identity: Stewardship of a living thing that cannot be told what to do. A hive is not harvested so much as kept: read the flowers around it, read the weight of the frames, read whether the colony is growing or quietly dying, and act a season before the answer becomes obvious. The comb is only the receipt. The skill is everything that had to go right in the eleven months before it.
BEE.mastery: A Grandmaster reads a site before setting a hive on it, and reads the frames before deciding what the colony can spare. The comb follows from that judgement rather than from anything done at the hive on the day.
BEE.tip: Flowers are the whole account. A hive set among too few will bleed population every day no matter how carefully you tend it, and no amount of feeding covers a bad site. Site well first, then keep. Take comb with an eye on what the colony needs to hold, not on what the frames will give you today: a hive robbed bare in autumn is a hive you will not have in spring.
